title: The Trade Marks Act, 1999 and Trade Marks Rules, 2017

sections.heading: Absolute Grounds for Refusal - Descriptive Traditional Names
sections.text: Trade marks which consist exclusively of marks or indications which may serve in trade to designate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, values, geographical origin or the time of production of the goods or of rendering of the service, or other characteristics of the goods or service, shall not be registered.
sections.relevance: Prevents monopolizing classical Sanskrit Ayurvedic herb names (e.g., 'Ashwagandha Churna', 'Triphala Guggulu') as exclusive proprietary brand names.

sections.heading: Relative Grounds for Refusal - Deceptive Similarity and Well-Known Marks
sections.text: A trade mark shall not be registered if because of its identity with an earlier trade mark and similarity of goods or services, there exists a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public, or where it takes unfair advantage of the reputation of a well-known mark.
sections.relevance: Protects established Ayurvedic brand names from deceptive imitation and unfair competition.

sections.heading: Prohibition of Registration of Names of Chemical Elements or INN
sections.text: Prohibits registration of generic botanical names, International Nonproprietary Names (INN), or commonly accepted Ayurvedic formulation names.
sections.relevance: Ensures public domain traditional medicinal terms remain accessible to all manufacturers.

sections.heading: Rights Conferred by Registration
sections.text: Registration of a trade mark shall, if valid, give to the registered proprietor the exclusive right to the use of the trade mark in relation to the goods or services in respect of which the trade mark is registered and to obtain relief in respect of infringement.
sections.relevance: Confers statutory exclusive commercial monopoly to the registered Ayurvedic brand.

sections.heading: Infringement of Registered Trade Marks - Identical Goods and Trade Dress
sections.text:
(1) A registered trade mark is infringed by a person who, not being a registered proprietor or permitted user, uses in the course of trade a mark which is identical with or deceptively similar to the trade mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered.
(2) Infringement occurs where identity or similarity of mark and goods creates likelihood of confusion or association.
(4) Infringement extends to detrimental use or taking unfair advantage of distinctive character or repute of a well-known mark.
(7) A person infringes by applying a mark to packaging, material intended for labelling, or advertising without authorization.
sections.relevance: Primary statutory remedy against copycat Ayurvedic products, deceptive imitation of distinctive bottle design, and trade dress infringement.

sections.heading: Representation of Trade Mark - Visual Representation and Logo
sections.text: Every application for the registration of a trade mark shall contain a clear and legible representation of the trade mark. Where a trade mark contains a device, logo, label, or distinctive shape of goods, the representation shall clearly depict the distinctive graphic features.
sections.relevance: Procedural rule governing depiction of distinctive Ayurvedic brand logos, devices, and label shapes.

sections.heading: Applicable Trademark Classes for Ayurvedic Startups
sections.text:
- Class 5: Ayurvedic medicines, classical ASU preparations, dietary supplements for medical purposes, herbal pharma.
- Class 3: Ayurvedic cosmetics, herbal soaps, essential oils, dhoop, hair oils, skincare.
- Class 30: Herbal teas, spices, confectionery, Ayurveda Aahara foods.
- Class 32: Ayurvedic non-alcoholic wellness beverages, herbal syrups, tonics.
- Class 44: Ayurvedic clinics, Panchakarma centers, wellness resorts, AYUSH telehealth.
sections.relevance: Direct class filing guidance for brand strategy.
